description: Welcome to Cosmic Troops! We are a dynamic team based out of Erode, currently tackling the Space Mission Design Game challenge. We are passionate about gamifying space concepts and are actively looking for enthusiastic minds to join us. Our core focus spans software development, coding, and web development. To bring our game's universe to life, we are looking for teammates skilled in hardware integration, graphic design, and animation. If you speak English and want to build an epic space game.
summary:
Mission Architect is a browser-based space mission design game. Players start with a science objective, then design the spacecraft: instruments, power, antenna, safety systems and fuel. They choose a launch vehicle, a launch window and a transfer trajectory. They then launch in 3D and make in-flight decisions, such as responding to solar flares, navigation errors, full data recorders and thermal faults. A final report scores the mission. One to four players can play, each with their own role.

It addresses the challenge by turning NASA’s mission-design resources into gameplay: the four mission segments, Concept Maturity Levels, Mission Design Lab study levels, GMAT-style delta-v and trajectory comparison, Mission Viz-style 3D views, and the telescope game’s idea that objectives limit instrument, wavelength and optics choices.

It matters because it shows students that every mission choice has a cost somewhere else, and that science goals drive engineering decisions. Every value is tagged as NASA, industry or estimate, so players can see what is real data.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mission Architect is a browser game where players design and fly a robotic space mission. They start with a science objective, which limits the instruments, wavelengths and optics they can choose. They then build the spacecraft (propulsion, power, antenna, safety systems, fuel), pick a launch vehicle, and choose a launch window and transfer trajectory. A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. The game compares delta-v by launch window, draws the transfer orbit, and has an Optimise button that finds the fastest trajectory with a 5% spare. Players then launch in 3D and make in-flight decisions, such as responding to a solar flare, a navigation error, a full data recorder, a passing comet or a thermal fault. A final report scores the mission and includes a user-segment line showing how much data reached scientists.

Benefits
Players learn that science goals drive engineering choices and that every trade-off has a cost elsewhere. It follows NASA’s mission-design ideas: the four mission segments, Concept Maturity Levels, the Mission Design Lab study levels, GMAT-style trajectory analysis, Mission Viz-style 3D views, and the telescope game’s idea that objectives limit choices.

Intended impact
We want students and space enthusiasts to see how real missions are planned, in a way they can try for themselves. Because every value is tagged as NASA, industry or estimate, players can tell what is real data and what is a game assumption.

Tools and technology
The game is a single HTML file written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses Three.js (r128) with bloom and anti-aliasing effects for the 3D scenes, and Google Fonts (Space Grotesk and IBM Plex Mono). It needs no special hardware and runs in a normal web browser. The game’s design and code were developed with help from an AI assistant. If the challenge requires you to disclose AI use, say so here.

Creativity
The game turns NASA’s reference material into play. Decisions happen in flight, not only in menus, and random events make each launch different. Locked options explain why they are locked, so players learn the reason instead of just hitting a wall. Teams of one to four players take separate roles.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy: sources panel and NASA, industry and estimate tags on every value.
  • Learning: three difficulty levels and clear reasons for locked options.
  • Teamwork: separate roles, sign-offs and design codes for comparing missions.
  • Replay value: random events, a sandbox mode and a leaderboard.
  • Honesty about limits: the trajectory tool compares a few options and is not a full optimiser.
